newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian stocks ease off highs on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Australian stocks ease off highs on profit-taking.

text.p: Profit-taking and a fall on Wall Street saw Australian stocks pull back on Tuesday, giving up most of Monday's gains although the market remains near its highs.
The All Ordinaries Index ended down 12.1 points at 2,613.6, near its lows for the day after a short-lived rally towards positive territory around the midsession.
"There's been some profit-taking in this market," said Shaw Stockbroking dealer Jamie Spiteri.
"The noticeable falls were in the resources sector...and the broader market was easier."

Dealers said the market had taken some of its early tone from Monday's fall on Wall Street, while investors were keen to take profits after a rally which has seen the All Ordinaries gain more than 80 points in the past two-and-half weeks.
Overall, falls outnumbered gains seven to six, while traders said turnover of A$1.04 billion belied a fairly quiet day.
The All Resources Index declined 0.94 percent, with Australia's biggest company the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) falling 28 cents to A$18.87.
Major miners, Rio Tinto Ltd and WMC Ltd were also weaker.
Westpac Banking Corp headed the turnover table, easing 20 cents to A$6.92 after going ex-dividend 19 cents with 9.3 million shares changing hands.
Other banks were mixed, with ANZ Ltd easing 13 cents to A$9.12 after Monday's strong rise after its better than expected first half profits.
Investment banking group Macquarie Bank Ltd hit a new high, jumping 50 cents to A$10.00 following Monday's stronger than expected annual profits.
Rural services group Iama Ltd rose seven cents to A$2.93 after reporting a nine percent rise in interim net profits.
Most market sectors recorded declines on the day, although property trusts remained in the black, supported by Australia's low interest rates.
Fosters Brewing Group ended steady on turnover of 5.9 million shares following renewed speculation about a possible A$2.5 billion share buy-back.
